# Exact polygonization of a common homothetic boundary arc

This is a local replacement lemma. It does not prove that a mixed extremizer
has the required common arcs, or that its contact pattern has finitely many
intervals.

## Single-arc lemma

Let K be a planar convex body. Let I be a closed interval of outward normal
angles of length less than pi. Suppose the portion of its boundary with
normals in I is a convex arc with distinct endpoints, and the body is left
unchanged outside this arc. There are replacements by polygonal convex arcs,
arbitrarily close to the original arc, that preserve its signed area relative
to the fixed endpoint chord. The replacement keeps the endpoints and the
support function outside the interior of I. Endpoint facets are allowed.

To prove this, take finitely many increasingly dense points on the arc,
including its endpoints. The inscribed polygonal arc lies on the interior
side of the original arc, shares its endpoints, and has no larger area
relative to the endpoint chord. Take also a sufficiently fine finite list
of supporting lines, including the endpoint supporting lines. Their
circumscribed polygonal arc lies on the exterior side and has no smaller
area. Both arcs converge to the original arc. They define convex bodies
K_in,K_out by retaining the rest of the original boundary. In support
coordinates their functions agree with h_K outside I. Endpoint facets of
the circumscribed arc create allowed positive curvature atoms at the
endpoints of I; they do not alter the outside support values.

For 0<=t<=1 the Minkowski interpolation

    K_t=(1-t)K_in+t K_out

still agrees with the original support function outside I. Inside I its
boundary is polygonal: the union of the finitely many edge normal directions
of the two replacement arcs is finite, and between consecutive such normals
both support functions are linear combinations of cos(theta),sin(theta).
Its endpoints stay fixed. Area is continuous under this interpolation and
straddles the original area at t=0,1. The intermediate value theorem supplies
the required exact area. All interpolants stay arbitrarily close to K.

If the arc is already a segment or is polygonal, no change is necessary.
One can instead work on a smaller closed subinterval of a regular arc, which
avoids questions about nonunique endpoint normals.

## Common-arc consequence for finitely many fibers

Suppose finitely many planar convex fibers have, on an open normal interval,
support functions of the form

    h_z(theta)=c_z h(theta)+a_z cos(theta)+b_z sin(theta),
    c_z>=0,

where c_z and the translation vectors (a_z,b_z) are fixed. On a smaller closed
subinterval apply the single-arc lemma to h, simultaneously replacing each
fiber's arc by the same translated and scaled polygonal arc. The area change
in fiber z is c_z^2 times the base arc area change, hence zero.

Suppose further that every fixed ambient cap under consideration has constant
membership on each affected fiber arc, with a positive separation from its
boundary. A sufficiently close replacement retains this membership. The cap
area change in that fiber is either its full arc area change or zero, so all
these cap areas are preserved exactly.

For finite support compatibility constraints, any equality that is respected
coefficientwise by the displayed c_z and translation vectors remains an
equality after replacement. Constraints with a uniform positive support gap
on the chosen subinterval remain valid for sufficiently close replacement.
Outside the subinterval all support functions are unchanged.

Thus this local construction preserves actual compatible fibers, their areas,
and all specified cap areas under the stated finite-gap and coefficient
hypotheses. These hypotheses must be proved before applying it. In particular,
the construction cannot replace unrelated curved arcs independently when a
support compatibility constraint is active between them.

## Algebraic check of the area scaling

For smooth support functions the local area expression is one half of
integral(h^2-(h')^2). The cross term introduced by a translation
l(theta)=a cos(theta)+b sin(theta) has change

    integral[l Delta h-l' Delta h']
       =integral[(l+l'')Delta h]-[l' Delta h]_(endpoints)=0,

because l+l''=0 and Delta h vanishes at the endpoints. The same identity
holds for piecewise smooth polygonal supports by integration by parts on the
pieces, or follows directly from translation invariance of the area between
two arcs sharing endpoints. The remaining change is exactly c_z^2 times the
base change.
